definition: Sanctimonious means showily virtuous in a hypocritical way.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sanctimonious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sanctimonious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her sanctimonious post about 'a weekend unplugged' went up from her phone, followed by three reminders to like it.
Moralizing lectures readily about right and wrong, but the lecturer may be sincere and even live by it; sanctimonious has left sincerity behind.
Self-righteous is the belief in one's own superior virtue; sanctimonious goes one rung further—wearing that virtue as a public costume, usually one the wearer doesn't live in.

Holier-than-thou behavior is openly acting morally superior to everyone around — the raised eyebrow at your lunch, the sigh at your shortcuts. Sanctimonious adds a darker claim: the virtue on display is a performance the preacher does not live. A holier-than-thou scold may practice what she preaches; the sanctimonious one only performs.

Preachy is about delivery: moral advice pressed on people constantly and tediously, whether or not the preacher is sincere. Sanctimonious condemns the substance as well as the style — the showy virtue is false, a halo polished in public but not worn at home. A devoted coach can be preachy without ever being sanctimonious.

Sanctimonious means showily virtuous in a hypocritical way.
Every morning Ted delivered a sanctimonious sermon on waste, inspecting the carpool's coffee cups for forbidden plastic.
Then his own trunk popped open at the gas station, and out rolled a case of bottled water—yet by Tuesday the sermons had resumed, holier than ever.
Sanctimonious targets the performance of virtue: the display, the lecture, the halo polished in public.
The plain word for the underlying gap is hypocrisy; sanctimonious describes how that gap sounds when it preaches.
Sanctimonious is never a compliment: it accuses someone of performing virtue—preaching, sighing, polishing a halo—without living it.
Hypocrisy, its partner in this unit, names the underlying gap between the preaching and the conduct; sanctimonious describes the showy lecture itself.
A sincere moralizer may be tiresome, but only the false show earns sanctimonious.

For three years, Walt Prentiss opened every town meeting with a speech about civic virtue, reminding his neighbors that character is what you do when nobody is watching.
He printed pledge cards for the river cleanup and wore a sash reading STEWARD at the spring parade.
Then a trail camera meant for deer caught a familiar pickup at the ravine, unloading paint cans and a torn sofa into the water he praised.
The clip made the rounds quietly.
At the next meeting, Walt rose to speak about character anyway, and the room heard the sanctimonious ring in every word.
But when he passed the pledge cards down the rows, they came back unsigned.
